title: The Sherry Triangle: Solera, Tabanco & the Bajo de Guía
subRegion: Marco de Jerez — Jerez de la Frontera, El Puerto de Santa María, Sanlúcar de Barrameda & Cádiz

bestPeriod.window: Late February–early June & late September–early November
bestPeriod.avoid: July–August (38–42°C inland, bodegas hot and half-staffed) and Feria del Caballo week in May, when Jerez prices double
bestPeriod.raw: Late February–early June & late September–early November

accommodation.note: Jerez palacete €90–€140 pppn; Sanlúcar and Cádiz €70–€120

food.note: Tabanco tapas €2.50–€5; Bajo de Guía langostinos €28–€45; one tasting menu €80–€120

transport.note: Regional trains, taxis between the three towns, one hired driver day

gatewayAirport: XRY Jerez, 15 min taxi to Jerez centre; SVQ Seville 1 h 15 min by car, 1 h 10 m by train
summary: Three towns, twenty kilometres apart, producing wines that cannot legally be made in each other's cellars. You spend the week learning why: albariza chalk, the flor yeast veil, the fractional blending of the solera, and the sea humidity that makes Sanlúcar's manzanilla thinner and saltier than Jerez's fino from identical grapes. Between visits it is a tapas trip — tabancos where a copa costs €1.60, Cádiz's Mercado Central, langostinos at the Guadalquivir mouth, retinto beef from the Vejer marshes. Cheap for what it is, and the most technically interesting wine week in Spain.

itinerary.title: Jerez: albariza, flor, first copa
itinerary.morning: Arrive at XRY, drop bags, and walk Jerez's old town to the Alcázar and the Cathedral of San Salvador, which stands above the historic bodega quarter.
itinerary.afternoon: The orientation visit at **González Byass (Tío Pepe)** — the Gustave Eiffel-attributed La Concha bodega, the venencia demonstration, and the Colors of Sherry flight covering fino through PX.
itinerary.evening: Tabanco crawl on Calle Santa María: **El Pasaje** for sherry from the butt and a 22:00 flamenco set, then **Tabanco Plateros** for chicharrones.
itinerary.dayStats: 1 bodega / González Byass tours €25.50–€50 / tabanco copa €1.60–€2.60, tapa €2.50–€4 / 15 min airport transfer
itinerary.sleep: Hotel Bodega Tío Pepe or Casa Palacio María Luisa, Jerez

itinerary.title: Old wines and the almacenista idea
itinerary.morning: **Bodegas Tradición** for VOS and VORS only — amontillado and palo cortado with 30-plus years of average age, plus the Zurbarán and Goya canvases upstairs.
itinerary.afternoon: **Bodegas Lustau** for the almacenista range, which bottles other people's soleras under their names — the clearest lesson in how the trade actually works.
itinerary.evening: **Mantúa** (Michelin-starred, Jerez) if you want the modern kitchen, or **Albalá** for a shorter, cheaper version of the same idea.
itinerary.dayStats: 2 bodegas / Tradición €40–€60, Lustau €18–€30 / VORS bottle band €55–€120 / all walking, no car
itinerary.sleep: Hotel Bodega Tío Pepe or Casa Palacio María Luisa, Jerez

itinerary.title: El Puerto de Santa María and the river bodegas
itinerary.morning: Train from Jerez to El Puerto (12 min). Visit **Gutiérrez Colosía**, whose butts sit metres from the Guadalete mouth — the humidity gives a visibly thicker flor than Jerez.
itinerary.afternoon: **Bodegas Osborne** and the Toro bull, then fried fish from a *freiduría* on Calle Misericordia, eaten in a paper cone with a copa from the bar next door, which is legal and expected.
itinerary.evening: **Aponiente**, Ángel León's three-star in a tidal mill on the salt marsh, if you booked months ago; otherwise **Romerijo** for a kilo of prawns.
itinerary.dayStats: Train €4 return / 2 bodegas / Colosía €18–€25 / freiduría cone €8–€14 / Aponiente tasting menu €250+
itinerary.sleep: Hotel Bodega Tío Pepe or Casa Palacio María Luisa, Jerez

itinerary.title: Sanlúcar: manzanilla and the Bajo de Guía
itinerary.morning: Transfer to Sanlúcar (35 min). **Barbadillo** in the Barrio Alto for Solear and the manzanilla pasada, then a walk down to the Barrio Bajo.
itinerary.afternoon: **La Guita** or **Hidalgo-La Gitana** for the second angle, then the Doñana view across the Guadalquivir from the Fábrica de Hielo.
itinerary.evening: **Casa Bigote** at Bajo de Guía: langostinos de Sanlúcar, acedías, and a cold half-bottle of manzanilla en rama that costs less than the starter.
itinerary.dayStats: 35 min transfer / 2 bodegas / fees €15–€30 / langostinos €28–€45 per ración / manzanilla bottle €7–€14
itinerary.sleep: Hotel Posada de Palacio, Sanlúcar de Barrameda

itinerary.title: Cádiz market day
itinerary.morning: Drive or bus to Cádiz (45 min) and go straight to the **Mercado Central de Abastos** — the Rincón Gastronómico stalls sell erizos, tuna mojama and a plate of gambas you eat standing up.
itinerary.afternoon: The sea wall from La Caleta to the Castillo de San Sebastián, then the **Torre Tavira** camera obscura for the peninsula's rooftop geography.
itinerary.evening: **Taberna Casa Manteca** in La Viña for chicharrón especial de Cádiz on waxed paper, then **El Faro de Cádiz** for a proper sit-down.
itinerary.dayStats: 45 min each way / market plates €3–€9 / Torre Tavira €8 / no bodega today, palate rest
itinerary.sleep: Hotel Posada de Palacio, Sanlúcar de Barrameda

itinerary.title: Vejer: retinto, vinegar and a kitchen
itinerary.morning: Drive inland to **Vejer de la Frontera**, a white hill town above the Barbate marshes, and take the cookery class at **Annie B's Spanish Kitchen** — tortillitas de camarones and a sherry reduction.
itinerary.afternoon: Retinto beef tasting at **Venta El Toro** or a visit to a sherry-vinegar solera at **Bodegas Páez Morilla** in Jerez on the way back, where the acetification bodega smells nothing like the wine one.
itinerary.evening: **Restaurante Trafalgar** on Vejer's Plaza de España, or back in Jerez at **Tabanco San Pablo**.
itinerary.dayStats: 60 min Sanlúcar–Vejer / class €75–€110, 4 h / vinegar visit €12–€20 / retinto steak €22–€32

itinerary.title: Pagos, horses and out
itinerary.morning: A vineyard morning, not a cellar one: ask a bodega to run you into the **Macharnudo** or **Balbaína** pago to see albariza chalk, white and spongy, holding winter rain through a rainless summer.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Real Escuela Andaluza del Arte Ecuestre** in Jerez for the Thursday or Friday "Cómo bailan los caballos andaluces" show, then last bottles at **La Casa del Jerez**.
itinerary.evening: Early flight from XRY, 15 minutes away, or the 1 h 10 m train to Seville.
itinerary.dayStats: Vineyard visit €25–€45 / equestrian show €22–€30 / XRY 15 min / duty-free sherry travels badly in the hold — pack upright
itinerary.sleep: Airport hotel or overnight in Seville

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Bodega Tío Pepe
accommodationStrategy.description: Inside the González Byass complex, so the Day 1 tour starts downstairs and you can walk to every tabanco on Calle Santa María. Rooms overlook the cellar courtyards; €120–€200 double.

accommodationStrategy.name: Casa Palacio María Luisa
accommodationStrategy.description: An eighteenth-century palace on Calle Tornería with a courtyard and a serious sherry list, two minutes from the cathedral. Better rooms, no bodega noise; €160–€260.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Posada de Palacio
accommodationStrategy.description: A converted eighteenth-century house minutes from Barbadillo and ten minutes' walk down to the Bajo de Guía seafood strip, which matters because you will not be driving after dinner. €80–€140 double.

logistics.connectivity: EU roaming, no surcharge. 4G/5G throughout; the only dead spots are inside thick-walled bodega naves.
logistics.emergency: 112, including Salvamento Marítimo for the Guadalquivir mouth. Hospital Universitario de Jerez is the main hospital; EHIC/GHIC accepted.
logistics.weather: Two winds define the trip. **Levante**, hot and easterly, dries the air and shrinks the flor; **poniente**, humid and westerly off the Atlantic, feeds it. Bodegas open windows for the poniente. Summer inland highs hit 42°C; Cádiz stays 8–10°C cooler.
logistics.bookingWindows: Aponiente 3–6 months. Bodegas Tradición 3–4 weeks by email. González Byass and Barbadillo 3–7 days online. Almacenista visits are arranged through Lustau or a specialist guide, not directly. Feria del Caballo hotels sell out six months out.
logistics.money: Eurozone. Cards work almost everywhere; tabancos and market stalls are quicker with coins. Tipping is minimal — round up, or 5–10% for a full restaurant meal.
logistics.transportRules: The Renfe C-1 line links Jerez, El Puerto and Cádiz cheaply and frequently; Sanlúcar has no rail service, only buses and taxis. Blood-alcohol limit is 0.5 g/l, 0.3 for drivers licensed under two years, and roadside checks around Jerez are routine. Parking inside Cádiz's old town is close to impossible — use the Canalejas underground car park.
logistics.permits: Bodega visits are timed and ticketed; walk-ins are refused at González Byass and Tradición. Shipping a case costs €25–€60 within Europe.
logistics.health: Tap water is drinkable across all three towns. Fino and manzanilla are 15% abv and drink deceptively like white wine — a tabanco round is stronger than it tastes. Sun on the Bajo de Guía sand is unshaded from noon.

proTips: Buy fino and manzanilla by bottling date, not vintage. Anything over a year old has lost the flor character you came for; the *saca* date is usually on the back label or the neck.
Do González Byass first and Bodegas Tradición second, never the reverse. The big tour teaches the solera mechanics you need to appreciate a 30-year VORS.

Order the same style in all three towns on consecutive days — fino in Jerez, fino-manzanilla in El Puerto, manzanilla in Sanlúcar — from the same producer where possible. That comparison is the whole trip in three glasses.
Ask to see the venencia used properly. In a real bodega the venenciador draws through the flor without breaking the veil, and the pour from arm's length is aeration, not theatre.
Tabancos are not tourist bars: they were wine shops that grew a counter. Order by the copa from the butt behind the bar rather than from the bottle list, and expect chalk marks instead of a receipt.
In Sanlúcar, eat at Bajo de Guía at 21:00, not 20:00. The langostinos land in the afternoon and the good places serve the day's catch late.
Sherry vinegar deserves a purchase alongside the wine. A Reserva vinegar from a solera costs €10–€18 and is the single most useful souvenir of the week.
If your dates fall near an *en rama* saca — March–April or September–October — ask the bodega to open one. It is the release that changes materially year to year.

raw.The DOs: **DO Jerez-Xérès-Sherry** and **DO Manzanilla-Sanlúcar de Barrameda** share a production zone but manzanilla may only be aged in Sanlúcar. **DO Vinagre de Jerez** covers the vinegars. Grapes: **Palomino Fino** for almost everything, **Pedro Ximénez** and **Moscatel** for the sweet wines. The best vineyards are **albariza** chalk in the pagos of Macharnudo, Balbaína, Carrascal and Añina — Macharnudo Alto is the grand cru.
raw.Styles: **Fino** and **manzanilla** age biologically under flor, 15–15.5% abv, and are living wines — buy the most recent bottling. **Amontillado** starts under flor and finishes oxidatively; **oloroso** never has flor, fortified to 17%+; **palo cortado** is the anomaly, the aromatics of amontillado with the body of oloroso. **PX** is raisined and sweet to 400+ g/l. **VOS** (aged over 20 years) and **VORS** (over 30) are certified by cask analysis. **En rama** means minimally filtered, released in seasonal *sacas*, usually spring and autumn.
raw.Solera and criadera: Butts stack in scales: the *solera* is the floor row wine is drawn from, the *criaderas* the rows above that replenish it. Fractional blending means no vintage exists and average age is a property of the extraction rate — ask each guide what percentage they draw a year.
raw.Bodegas, large and small: **González Byass (Tío Pepe)**, Calle Manuel María González 12, Jerez, books online at tiopepe.com: the Tío Pepe Experience around €25.50, Colors of Sherry €28.50, tapas versions €30.50–€33.50, and a Premium VORS tour at €50; Tuesday–Sunday, advance reservation required, English guides standard, phone +34 956 357 016. **Bodegas Tradición** (Jerez) is the counterpoint — VOS/VORS only plus a private Spanish painting collection, small groups, email weeks ahead, roughly €40–€60. **Bodegas Lustau** runs an almacenista programme. In Sanlúcar, **Barbadillo** sells tours online; **La Guita** and **Hidalgo-La Gitana** run smaller visits. In El Puerto, **Osborne** and riverfront **Gutiérrez Colosía**. *Almacenistas* — stockholders who age but never bottle — are the connoisseur's visit, arranged through Lustau or a specialist guide.
raw.Producers beyond wine: **Tabanco El Pasaje**, Calle Santa María 8, Jerez — the oldest surviving tabanco, sherry from the butt, daily flamenco. **Tabanco Plateros** and **Tabanco San Pablo** complete the crawl. **Casa Balbino** on Plaza del Cabildo, Sanlúcar, for tortillitas de camarones. **Casa Bigote** and **Joselito Huerta** at Bajo de Guía for langostinos de Sanlúcar. In Cádiz, the **Mercado Central de Abastos** and its Rincón Gastronómico stalls. **Venta El Toro** and **Trafalgar** in Vejer for retinto. Sherry vinegar at **Bodegas Páez Morilla** and Lustau's vinegar soleras.
raw.Season and timing: *Vendimia* runs mid-August to mid-September, brutally hot, with Jerez's **Fiesta de la Vendimia** in early September. *En rama* sacas land around March–April and September–October, the best weeks for flor wine. Avoid **Feria del Caballo** in May unless you want horses more than wine.
raw.Hands-on element and driving: A half-day class at **Annie B's Spanish Kitchen** in Vejer de la Frontera — tortillitas de camarones, a sherry reduction, retinto — €75–€110, English-taught, two weeks' notice. Spain's limit is 0.5 g/l (0.3 under two years' licence) and checks are routine. Use **Renfe** C-1: Jerez–El Puerto 12 min, Jerez–Cádiz 40 min, €4–€7. Sanlúcar has no station — taxi or the M-050 bus. **Sherry Explorers** and **Turismo Sabor** run English-speaking driver days at €280–€450 per car.
